title: Eight Weeks Toward a Decision You Can Live With
subtitle: An eight week plan from James Bell for the decision you can't seem to make and the fear of missing God's will. What God has already made plain, wisdom for the asking, honest counsel, and a date to decide by.
intro:
This is an eight week walk for the person standing at a fork who doesn't know which way to go: a job, a move, a person, a calling, or the larger question of what to do with your one life. Each week holds one focus, one small daily practice, one thing to read, one tool to use, and one honest question. It begins with the decision that keeps you up at night and goes beneath it to the fear of missing God's will. Then it takes up what Scripture actually gives: what God has already made plain, wisdom for the asking, honest counsel, and time to wait before you act. It ends with living with what you chose. If your decision can't wait eight weeks, don't make it wait; the care page in week one sets out steps you can walk in a week or two. If you've already chosen and can't stop second-guessing, week eight is the place to begin.

It is not a cure, and it is not a substitute for a doctor, a licensed counselor, a pastor, or the people who know and love you. If your decision involves your health, the law, or serious money, bring in a doctor, a lawyer, or a qualified financial professional before you choose; nothing here is that kind of advice. Walk it at your own pace. A missed week is not failure; you just pick it back up. These weeks can't make the decision for you, and they won't pretend it's small. They can help you make it honestly before God, with people beside you, in a way you can live with whichever road it opens.
careNote: If you haven't been able to make even small decisions for weeks, or fear of choosing wrong is costing you sleep or work, see a doctor or a licensed counselor, and in a crisis, call or text 988. If you're deciding whether to leave someone who frightens or hurts you, your safety comes first, and the Find Help page lists the Domestic Violence Hotline.

weeks.focus: Two futures at two in the morning
weeks.why: A big decision seldom arrives as a question about God's will. It arrives at two in the morning, with both futures playing out in your head until neither looks real, and a list of reasons for and against that you've rewritten so often it no longer tells you anything. A decision that lives only in your head grows larger than life, because a mind under pressure plays out every ending and can't rest in any of them. Written down in one plain sentence, it usually shrinks to its actual size. Under most hard decisions sits a fear as well, of choosing wrong and living for years with the regret, and the fear needs naming as much as the choice does. If you can't make even small decisions anymore, or the worry is costing you sleep, tell a doctor.
weeks.practice: On the first day, write the decision in one plain sentence, such as whether to take the new job or stay where you are, and under it write what you're afraid will happen if you choose wrong. Each day after that, read both sentences aloud to God and ask him for wisdom. When the two futures start running at night, write the worry down, name the one thing that is yours to do tomorrow, and go to sleep.

read.label: The care page on God's will and big decisions, with first steps and when to get more help

tool.label: The Worry Journal, five minutes before bed: the worry, the one thing yours to do tomorrow, and what isn't yours to carry

weeks.reflection: What is this decision really about for me: the choice itself, or what I'm afraid it will say about my life?

weeks.focus: The fear of missing God's will
weeks.why: For many people the hardest part of a big decision is the fear underneath it, that God has one right answer hidden somewhere and that missing it would leave them outside his will for good. Faithful Christians answer differently whether God has a particular path for each life, and the creeds don't settle it; the questions at the end of the care page from week one set out both answers with the texts behind them. Both agree that nothing in your life escapes God's knowledge and care. What fear adds, on either side, is a picture of his guidance as a code you must crack. Our age makes it heavier by treating every large choice as a verdict on who you are, and those of us who preach have sometimes made God's will sound like a scavenger hunt.
weeks.practice: Each day, notice when the decision starts to feel like a verdict on your whole life, and write down the sentence the fear is saying, something like: if I get this wrong, I'll have missed what God made me for. Beside it, write one thing that is true about God whichever road you take. On one day, read Proverbs 3:1-12 slowly. On another, read those questions at the end of the care page.

read.label: God's Sovereignty, on a Father who governs all things, and why that is comfort rather than fatalism

tool.label: The Passage Context tool, opened to Proverbs 3:5-6, the straight-paths verse read inside a father's counsel to his son

weeks.reflection: What have I assumed God will do if I choose wrong, and where did I learn to think of him that way?

weeks.why: When prayer meets silence, many of us start reading ordinary things as messages: a verse that turns up twice in a week, a delay that must mean something. The longing for a clear word is understandable, and God sometimes gives one. Yet the New Testament never tells believers to decide by asking for signs, and Gideon's fleece came after God had already told him what to do, as Gideon's own words admit (Judges 6:14, 36-37). There is humility in wanting a sign, and sometimes something else: a hope that if God decides for us, the outcome is his to answer for, or a need to see the end before taking the first step. In Deuteronomy, Moses tells Israel, "The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us" (Deuteronomy 29:29). Hunting for the hidden things is often easier than doing the plain ones.
weeks.practice: Each day, notice when you catch yourself looking for a sign, and write down what you hoped it would settle for you. Then ask honestly which you want more, God's guidance or relief from having to choose. On one day, read Judges 6 and notice how patient God is with Gideon's fear, and how plainly he had already spoken.

read.label: Hearing From God, on testing what you think you hear against what he has already said

tool.label: Judges 6 in the Study Bible, Gideon's fleece in its setting, with the hard question of whether Christians should put out fleeces

weeks.reflection: If God gave me the sign I've been asking for, what would I do with it that I couldn't do without it?

weeks.focus: What God has already made plain
weeks.why: Micah 6 sets a worshiper before God, bargaining. He offers calves, then thousands of rams, then rivers of oil, then his own firstborn, as if God were holding out for a higher price. The prophet's answer is plain: "He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?" (Micah 6:8). Most of God's will isn't hidden, and most of it concerns the kind of person you become, which is open to you on either road. So begin with what he has said. A road that requires deceiving someone, or abandoning a person who depends on you, is already closed. Of the roads still open, ask which would help you love God and your neighbor more truly (Matthew 22:37-39). The field is often narrower than fear made it look.
weeks.practice: On the first day, read Micah 6:1-8. Then write your options side by side, and under each, note what God has already said that bears on it: the promises you've made, the people who depend on you, any command that applies. Cross out any road that would mean deceiving or abandoning someone. Each day after, ask of each road still open which would help you love God and your neighbor more, and write one sentence about why.

read.label: Knowing God's Will, on how much of it is already revealed and rarely the thing we ask about

tool.label: Micah 6 in the Study Bible, where a worshiper keeps raising the offer and hears what God has already shown

weeks.reflection: What has God already made plain that I've been neglecting while I wait for him to tell me the rest?

weeks.why: The letter of James promises wisdom to anyone who asks, from a God "who gives generously to all without finding fault" (James 1:5). He won't scold you for asking a second time, or a tenth. The warning that follows, about the doubter tossed like a wave, has frightened many undecided Christians, but the letter uses the same word, double-minded, for people trying to keep friendship with the world and with God at once (James 4:4, 8). It warns a divided heart, not an honest one that simply doesn't know yet. Wisdom also grows by listening. Proverbs opens with a father handing his son a way of life. I was raised without a father, and many of us were. The book can still be that voice, if you'll sit with it a little every day.
weeks.practice: Each morning, ask God plainly for wisdom about your decision. If words won't come, borrow the ones King Jehoshaphat prayed before an army too big for him: "We do not know what to do, but our eyes are upon You" (2 Chronicles 20:12). Then read the chapter of Proverbs that matches today's date, and copy out one verse that bears on how you are deciding, not only on what.

read.label: What Proverbs and Ecclesiastes teach about wisdom, beginning with the decision the Bible did not cover

tool.label: Proverbs in 31 Days, the chapter that matches today's date, with a verse worth keeping and a question to carry

weeks.reflection: Have I been asking God for wisdom, or only for an answer, and what would change if I asked for the first?

weeks.why: When King Rehoboam had to answer his people, he asked the elders who had served his father, set their advice aside, and took the harsher counsel of the young men he had grown up with. The kingdom split (1 Kings 12:6-20). It matters whom you ask, and whether you want counsel or permission. Choose two or three people who know you well, know their Bibles, and have nothing to gain from what you decide, and tell them everything, especially the part you'd prefer they didn't hear. "Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed" (Proverbs 15:22). If you're married, your spouse isn't one of the advisers. Your spouse is inside the decision with you, since you will both live whatever you choose. And be wary of anyone, a pastor like me included, who claims God told them what you must do.
weeks.practice: Each day, pray by name for two or three people who could counsel you, and before the week ends ask each for an unhurried conversation. Tell them the decision, the facts, and your fears, and ask what they see that you don't. If you're married, talk it through with your spouse first and pray about it together. If you're afraid of your spouse, your safety comes first: talk alone with someone at the Domestic Violence Hotline on the Find Help page.

read.label: How to Find a Mentor, on asking someone further down the road for one small, specific conversation

tool.label: 1 Kings 12 in the Study Bible, where a new king sets aside the elders' advice and follows the friends he grew up with

weeks.reflection: Whose counsel have I been avoiding because I suspect what they'll say, and what does that suspicion tell me?

weeks.why: Some waiting is wisdom. "He who hurries his footsteps misses the mark" (Proverbs 19:2), and a choice made in a panic usually shows it. Ignatius of Loyola, in the sixteenth century, taught people to notice what draws them toward God and what drags them toward darkness and unrest, which he called desolation, and he counseled never to reverse a decision in such a time. But waiting needs an end, or it quietly becomes a decision of its own. "He who watches the wind will fail to sow" (Ecclesiastes 11:4). When the young church had to settle whether Gentile believers must keep the law of Moses, it described its judgment with modesty: "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us" (Acts 15:28). Those are the words of people who listened to one another and to the Scriptures, reasoned together, and then acted.
weeks.practice: Choose a date by which you will decide, near enough that the question can't hang open forever, and tell someone what it is. Until then, gather the facts you still lack: the costs, the deadlines, what each road means for the people who depend on you. Each evening, picture yourself on each road for a few minutes and notice what draws you toward God and what pulls you away. On the date, decide, tell that person what you chose, and take the first concrete step.

read.label: How to Wait on God, on waiting that stays awake, neither forcing God's hand nor going numb

tool.label: Ecclesiastes 11 in the Study Bible, the Teacher's case for sowing when no one knows which seed will succeed

weeks.reflection: Am I waiting because there is something left to learn, or because choosing means living with what I chose?

weeks.focus: Living with the road you chose
weeks.why: Once you've chosen, the temptation is to keep choosing, reopening at midnight what you settled in daylight. New facts can be a reason to revisit a decision with your counselors; a bad night is not. Every real choice closes a door, and the road you didn't take may deserve some grief, which is different from relitigating it. If the road turns hard, that doesn't prove you missed God, since Scripture is full of hard roads walked by faithful people. If your choice involved sin, confess it and make what amends you can; God forgives. If you chose one good thing over another, you haven't stepped outside his care. "A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps" (Proverbs 16:9). You did the planning, as you should have. The steps were always his.
weeks.practice: When the urge to re-decide comes, especially at night, write down what you're afraid of, pray it, and set it aside until you can talk with one of your counselors in daylight. Each day, take one small step that commits you to the road you chose. By the end of the week, write on a card the steps that helped you decide this time, and keep it for the next fork.

read.label: Regret and the Past, on the regret that leads back to God and the kind that only circles the wound

tool.label: The Prayer Planner, give the decision and the people it touches a day of the week, and keep a dated record

weeks.reflection: What will I need to remember about God on the day this road gets hard, and who will remind me of it?
